newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS - EU ministers edges towards farm price deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU ministers edges towards farm price deal.

text.p: European Union farm ministers were moving on Wednesday, the third day of annual price fixing negotiations, towards agreement on a package of measures for the coming year, EU officials said.
They said ministers broadly supported a Dutch EU Presidency compromise postponing a controversial proposal to slash aid to wheat farmers, but various details remained to be settled.
"We should get agreement this afternoon after some minor changes," a Dutch spokesman said.
"The reaction was reasonably positive," added a Commission spokesman during a break in the meeting.
France's new farm minister Louis Le Pensec said French demands on cereals set-aside, beef and other items had been met.
"If this compromise is adopted it would mean mission accomplished on all fronts," he told reporters.
But Germany and several other countries did not want to prejudge future farm reforms to prepare for the EU's expansion eastwards and the next round of World Trade Organisation talks.
They opposed any pledge of future cuts in grain compensation payments and wanted to change the wording of the text to say that cuts were "not necessary" instead of "premature".
The six-page Dutch text contained a series of "sweeteners" demanded by ministers for sugar, milk, beef, and other products. Spain had the most unsatisfied requests.
Key demands in the text were for the cereals set-aside rate to be maintained at five percent in 1998 and for a suspension of penalties on farmers who over-planted for another two years.
The EU's embattled farm chief, Franz Fischler, had said it was too early to make such decisions.
Set-aside is a scheme intended to remove costly grain mountains, under which farmers must take a certain percentage of their land out of production to obtain EU subsidies.
Under so-called penalty set-aside, farmers have to take extra land out of production if they exceed planting limits.

Regarding cereals subsidies, Fischler has insisted on a 1.4 billion Ecus ($1.6 billion) cut in the payments, which mainly benefit wealthy grain producers in Britain, France and Germany, to help finance extra aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow disease crisis.

The Commission estimated that grain farmers, who already receive the lion's share of EU farm subsidies, were over-paid by 8.5 billion Ecus during the past four years for cuts in support prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms.

But an overwhelming majority of farm ministers disputed this estimate, adding it was unfair to make cereals farmers foot the bill and that there was enough spare cash in the 1997 budget to aid beef producers.

The Dutch text did, however, concede that the compensatory payments have not been adjusted since 1992 and that "market prices have, on balance, been higher than those foreseen at the time of the reform."
Prices soared after bad weather hit crops across the world and grain stocks slumped to the lowest level for 20 years.

Commission officials noted that the draft deal contained a pledge to keep spending within the farm budget and warned that reductions might have to be made in every sector if the cereals cuts were shelved.
